paragraphs.heading: Three-lobed sea creatures
paragraphs.text: Trilobites, whose name means "three-lobed entities", are extinct arthropods that lived in the sea and form the class Trilobita. They were one of the earliest arthropod groups to show up in the fossil record and among the most successful early animals. They lived in the oceans for almost 270 million years, and more than 22,000 species have been described. The biggest grew over 70 centimetres long and may have weighed up to 4.5 kilograms.

paragraphs.heading: Built to fossilize
paragraphs.text: Their exoskeleton was mineralized with calcite, and it fossilized easily. Together with their great variety, this left a huge fossil record. Studying it has helped biostratigraphy, paleontology, evolutionary biology and plate tectonics. Trilobites belong to a wider group called Artiopoda, whose other members looked similar but lacked heavy mineral shells, so they are usually found only in exceptionally preserved deposits, mostly from the Cambrian.

paragraphs.heading: Many ways to make a living
paragraphs.text: Trilobites spread into many ecological niches. Some crawled over the seabed as predators, scavengers or filter feeders, while others swam and ate plankton. Nearly every lifestyle seen in sea arthropods today appears among them, with parasitism still under debate. Some, especially the family Olenidae, may even have teamed up with sulfur-eating bacteria and drawn food from them. A common trend over time was effacement, the loss of surface detail on parts of the shell, which is thought to point to burrowing or to life in open water.

paragraphs.heading: Fast rise in the Cambrian
paragraphs.text: The moment trilobites first appear in the rocks is used to mark the start of a time unit, Cambrian Stage 3, around 521 million years ago. They showed up at roughly the same time in Laurentia, Siberia and West Gondwana. Very soon after, they split into the major orders typical of the Cambrian. Their variety peaked in the late Cambrian and Ordovician and stayed high through the Silurian and early Devonian.

paragraphs.heading: A long decline
paragraphs.text: In the middle and late Devonian a string of extinction events, among them the Kellwasser and Hangenberg events, wiped out most trilobite variety. Only one order, Proetida, survived. Trilobites bounced back a little in the Early Carboniferous, then stayed at low numbers through the late Carboniferous and Permian, though they were still found widely. The last of them vanished in the end-Permian mass extinction about 251.9 million years ago, when only a handful of species were left.

paragraphs.heading: Rare glimpses of soft parts
paragraphs.text: Three specimens of Megistaspis hammondi from Morocco, 478 million years old, still hold fossilized soft parts. In 2024 researchers described soft tissues, including the labrum, in trilobites from Cambrian Stage 4 rocks in Morocco. These animals were probably preserved so well because they died quickly after an underwater pyroclastic flow.
